items.body: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.  Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. items.summary: "نحن فخورون بالفوز اليوم"
items.body: "نحن فخورون بالفوز اليوم" شكل فوز برشلونة الصعب بنتيجة 2-1 على أتلتيكو مدريد دفعة معنوية كبيرة للاعبي البلوجرانا، وهو ما أكده جافي، نجم البارسا، بعد المباراة على ملعب واندا ميتروبوليتانو. وتحدث جافي إلى وسائل الإعلام التابعة لبرشلونة ، ولم يتردد في التأكيد على أهمية الفوز، خاصةً بالنظر إلى الأداء القوي للفريق في الشوط الثاني. وقال: "كان فوزًا بالغ الأهمية بالنسبة لنا. لقد كانت مباراة حاسمة للفريق، ونحن سعداء للغاية بتحقيق هذا الفوز. سنحت لهم فرص، لكن الأمر يتعلق بتسجيل الأهداف. عرفنا كيف نستغل فرصنا، ونحن فخورون بالفوز اليوم". وواصل: "إنه فوز جاء بفضل الجميع. سيطرنا على الشوط الثاني بشكل ممتاز. أدرنا المباراة بشكل جيد، وهذا أمر مهم بالنسبة لنا كلاعبين شباب. لقد تحسنّا في جوانب عديدة. أنا سعيد جدًا للفريق". ولم يتردد جافي، في الإشارة إلى أن أتلتيكو مدريد "خصم عنيد لأنهم يعرفون كيف يلعبون ضدنا جيدًا". ناقش الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة وتابع: "لقد أثبتوا ذلك مجدداً اليوم. لديهم الأدوات اللازمة لإلحاق ضرر كبير بنا. هذه المباريات ضد أتلتيكو صعبة للغاية. إنها أشبه بالحرب لأن الأجواء فيها متوترة، بل هي الأكثر توتراً في أوروبا. كان من المهم جداً بالنسبة لنا تحقيق الفوز".

items.summary: الحارس كاريوس يغادر المباراة
items.body: الحارس كاريوس يغادر المباراة شهدت مواجهة شالكه وهوفنهايم، التي انتهت بفوز الأخير (2-1)، ضمن منافسات الدوري الألماني، لحظات مرعبة خلال الشوط الثاني، بعدما تعرض الحارس لوريس كاريوس لإصابة قوية في الرأس إثر اصطدام عنيف بزميله روبن جوسينس، ما استدعى توقف المباراة لعدة دقائق وسط حالة من القلق بين اللاعبين والجماهير. وسلطت صحيفة " بيلد " الألمانية الضوء على الواقعة، التي حدثت في الدقيقة 47، بعدما سدد فيسنيك أسلاني كرة قوية من مسافة 14 مترًا، لم يتمكن كاريوس من السيطرة عليها، ليتدخل جوسينس لإبعادها، لكن الحارس اندفع في اللحظة نفسها، فاصطدمت ساق زميله الممدودة برأسه، ليسقط أرضًا متأثرًا بالإصابة. وظل كاريوس ملقى على أرض الملعب لعدة دقائق، وسط تدخل الطاقم الطبي لتقديم الإسعافات اللازمة، فيما خيم الصمت على أرجاء الملعب، وتوقفت الجماهير عن التشجيع، بينما بدأ كيفن مولر، الحارس البديل لشالكه، الاستعداد للمشاركة تحسبًا لعدم قدرة الحارس الأساسي على استكمال اللقاء. وتعرض كاريوس لجرح في الأنف، لكنه تمكن في النهاية من مغادرة الملعب سيرًا على قدميه، ليحل مولر بديلًا له، في الوقت الذي كشفت فيه الواقعة عن إصابة أخرى تعرض لها جوسينس، بعدما التوت ركبته خلال الاصطدام بجسد الحارس، واضطر إلى مغادرة الملعب وهو يعرج، مع وضع ضمادة سميكة على ركبته، ليشارك فيتالي بيكر بدلًا منه. The birth of the Gulf of California, which rifted from Mexico and created the Baja Peninsula 6 million to 8 million years ago, was accelerated by the formation of a double subduction zone more than 6,000 miles (9,600 kilometers) away, near Japan. This reorganization led to a transfer of tectonic force across the Pacific tectonic plate, which, in turn, opened the Gulf of California and ultimately led to the Grand Canyon's formation, according to new research published Oct. 29 in the journal Science . items.title: 50% of long COVID patients show improvement in 3 years — but the condition tends to linger in those with this subtype
items.summary: About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.
items.body: Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness. That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems. In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine , roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame. This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems. items.title: Perfectly preserved owl fossil from 47 million years ago could help to solve a major evolutionary mystery
items.summary: A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.
items.body: A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds. The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga . Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach. The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study. items.title: Scientists removed the glare from a James Webb telescope image — and unmasked a hidden planet
items.summary: Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their star's glare.
items.body: When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature . "Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez , an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement . "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare." Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. items.body: Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis. In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science , researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a " spectral cavalcade ," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis , a wild type of cannabis or marijuana. Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting. Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure. Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination. This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study. High-resolution GPS tracking showed him moving parallel to four lanes of roaring traffic, bouncing off the highway like a furry pinball as he searched for a gap. Eventually, Lingenpolter beat the odds, probably by slipping under a river bridge. But his hero's journey shows what a formidable barrier a busy highway can be for wildlife, Cecily Costello , a research wildlife biologist at Montana's Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks, told Live Science. "It is easy to imagine the difficulty this grizzly bear experienced trying to reach the other side," Costello said. items.title: One-third of babies diagnosed with peanut allergy don't actually have one, study hints
items.summary: New findings suggest that "food challenges" can help prevent children from being saddled with unnecessary allergy diagnoses.
items.body: A peanut allergy diagnosis in infancy can mean years of avoiding the food or undergoing treatments to build tolerance. But a recent study suggests that more than one-third of babies thought to have the allergy may stop reacting badly to peanuts within months of that diagnosis. In an analysis published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice , researchers conducted supervised "food challenges" with infants diagnosed with a peanut allergy. These challenges involved giving the babies increasing amounts of peanut protein, with the intention of confirming whether they indeed had an allergy. The team found that more than 1 in 3 infants who underwent the food challenge tolerated the peanut protein, meaning they didn't experience symptoms of an allergic reaction. "This rate is much higher than we thought," study co-author Dr. Timothy Brettig , a pediatric allergist at the National Allergy Centre of Excellence in Australia, told Live Science. items.title: Physicists sank a telescope 1.5 miles under the sea to put Einstein's relativity to the test
items.summary: A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.
items.body: The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible. (Image credit: Edward Berbee/Nikhef) A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks. The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA) , detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France. Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move. The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments. items.title: A tiny chunk of Australia seeded Southeast Asia's tropical forests 50 million years ago, plant fossils preserved in amber reveal
items.summary: An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.
items.body: Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports. The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago. At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia. After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said. Scientists find the best evidence yet of potentially habitable volcanic vents on Mars
items.summary: Magma and a possible environment for ancient life might be present on Mars in the region of a large volcano on the Red Planet.
items.body: A noxious gas found seeping through cracks on Mars hints that there may be magma flowing beneath the Red Planet's surface — and perhaps even an environment similar to habitable ones on Earth, a new study suggests. Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft spotted a possible signal of hydrogen chloride gas leaking from rifts in the region of Alba Mons, the largest volcano on Mars in terms of surface area. (Mars' famous Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in terms of height.) Scientists interpret this gas as emissions from hot magma below the regolith of Mars. Although more research is required to confirm the emissions, the team suggested that Alba Mons may host an environment similar to hydrothermal vents on Earth, where life once likely arose and continues to thrive today. The study, published in the journal Science Advances Wednesday (Nov. 4), is not the first to suggest that magma may be flowing on Mars; NASA's InSight lander interpreted its presence through seismic observations and modeling earlier this year . items.title: This self-powered toothbrush makes electricity to kill cavity-causing bacteria
items.summary: Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.
items.body: A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease. Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth. "It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics , an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting." The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. items.title: Southern Taurid meteor shower could bring fireballs ‪this week —‬ when and where to look
items.summary: The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.
items.body: One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower. Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA , fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus . The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5. Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time. items.title: When dinosaurs are sold to the highest bidder, we all lose
items.summary: The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history, say Kristi Curry Rogers and Lindsay Zanno.
items.body: Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place. On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024. Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors. There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. items.summary: A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.
items.body: The patient: A woman in upstate New York The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes. The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case , which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program. Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. However, no new details on reentry have been provided. Stay tuned for more updates about where and when the telescope will fall. NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth any moment now, the space agency says. According to NASA's latest estimates , shared Monday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft was likely to reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could have plunged down as early as Tuesday evening, and as late as Wednesday afternoon. An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit , similarly estimates that the telescope should have reentered the atmosphere at 6:56 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take three hours. items.summary: Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.
items.body: Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints. The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One , found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis , which is known to increase the risk of heart failure. This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation. But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats ( 80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth. items.title: Traces of ancient blood found in 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil, new study claims
items.summary: Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.
items.body: Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims. However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells. In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS , the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin. The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali . While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils , this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones. "Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice , a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin Unive…

items.title: Buried for 2,600 years beneath Nile mud, a massive ancient Egyptian complex was just found — from space
items.summary: Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.
items.body: Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself. The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians , it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape. Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table. items.title: Blue whales have gone missing off the Galápagos. Scientists think El Niño could be why.
items.summary: Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.
items.body: For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale. The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year. This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing. Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant. items.title: Webb and Hubble discover new details in one of our galaxy's spookiest objects
items.summary: The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.
items.body: In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes. Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid . items.title: How do summers differ between Earth's hemispheres?
items.summary: Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?
items.body: Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer. Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same? Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts. The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA , this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun . This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere. items.title: Astronomers may have been wrong about what ended the 'Cosmic Dark Age'
items.summary: How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.
items.body: The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today. Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang , the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light. Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe." items.title: Are sharks really older than trees?
items.summary: It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?
items.body: You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years. But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark. "It's all in the fine print," John Maisey , the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark." The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes , an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin. items.body: While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside. The findings , presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations. In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.
